learn.hook: If you know the secret rule, you can predict a number nobody has written yet. That's maths magic!
points: A number sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule, like 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
To find the rule, look at how each number changes into the next: do we add, subtract, multiply or double?
Famous sequences: counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ...; odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ...; powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...
Virahānka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... : each number is the sum of the two numbers before it.

example.q: Find the next two numbers: 3, 7, 11, 15, ...
steps: The gaps are 7 − 3 = 4, 11 − 7 = 4, 15 − 11 = 4, so the rule is 'add 4'.

learn.reallife: Seat numbers in a train coach, house numbers on one side of a street (1, 3, 5, ...) and saving money that doubles all follow number sequences.

games.title: Match each sequence to its rule

quiz.q: What comes next: 4, 9, 14, 19, ...?
quiz.explain: Each number is 5 more than the one before, so 19 + 5 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the wrong gap (4 or 6) or adds 10 instead of 5

quiz.q: Riya saves ₹1 on day 1, ₹2 on day 2, ₹4 on day 3, doubling every day. How much does she save on day 6?
quiz.explain: Doubling each day gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Day 6 is ₹32.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 each day instead of doubling, or counts one day too many or too few

quiz.q: The Virahānka numbers go 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... What is the next number?
quiz.explain: Each Virahānka number is the sum of the two before it, so 8 + 13 = 21.
steps: The two numbers before are 8 and 13
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed gap of 5 or doubles 13 instead of adding the last two numbers

quiz.q: Which number is missing: 81, 27, ___, 3, 1?
quiz.explain: Each number is the one before divided by 3: 27 ÷ 3 = 9, and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 fits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rule is 'subtract' instead of 'divide by 3'

quiz.q: Add the first five odd numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = ?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25. Adding the first five odd numbers always gives 5 × 5, a square number.
quiz.mistake: Makes an adding slip or multiplies 5 × 4 or 5 × 6

quiz.q: Meena writes 100, 92, 84, 76, ... What is the 6th number in her list?
quiz.explain: The rule is 'subtract 8'. The list goes 100, 92, 84, 76, 68, 60, so the 6th number is 60.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 5th number (68) or goes one step too far (52)

quiz.q: Which sequence follows the rule 'multiply by 2'?
quiz.explain: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24. The others add 2, add 3 or multiply by 3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3, 6, 9, 12 doubles because 3 to 6 is a double, without checking the next step

quiz.q: Cubes go 1, 8, 27, 64, ... What is the next cube?
quiz.explain: The 5th cube is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
quiz.mistake: Works out 5 × 5 (a square) instead of 5 × 5 × 5

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Someone gave me 5, 10, 15, 20... How do I find the next number?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Find the rule, then use it again. I can predict numbers now!
teach.nudge: But how do I know what to do to get from one number to the next?

learn.hook: Pictures can hide number patterns. Count the sides, dots or lines, and a sequence pops out!
points: In a shape pattern, count something in each picture: sides, corners, dots, lines or small squares.
Regular polygons: triangle (3 sides), square (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), heptagon (7), octagon (8). The sides are the counting numbers from 3.
Square grids of size 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, ... have 1, 4, 9, ... small squares: the square numbers.
Join every pair of dots with lines: 2 dots need 1 line, 3 dots need 3, 4 dots need 6, 5 dots need 10: the triangular numbers.
Koch snowflake: each step turns every line into 4 smaller lines, so the line count goes 3, 12, 48, 192 (times 4 each step).

example.q: How many lines are needed to join every pair of 6 dots?
steps: The 6th dot must be joined to each of the 5 old dots: 5 new lines.

learn.reallife: Rangoli designs, tiles on a floor and patterns on saris often grow in steps that follow number patterns.

games.title: Odd or even number of sides?

Square
Pentagon

games.title: Shape pattern facts
items: A hexagon has 6 sides.
Hexa means six.
A 3×3 grid has 6 small squares.
It has 3 rows of 3, which is 9 small squares.
Joining every pair of 4 dots needs 6 lines.
In the Koch snowflake, each step multiplies the number of lines by 4.
Every line is replaced by 4 smaller lines.
A pentagon has 6 corners.
A pentagon has 5 sides and 5 corners.
A regular octagon has 8 sides and 8 corners.
Any polygon has as many corners as sides.

quiz.q: Arjun draws regular polygons in order: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, ... How many sides does the shape after the hexagon have?
quiz.explain: Each shape has one more side than the one before. A hexagon has 6, so the next shape (a heptagon) has 7.
quiz.mistake: Skips a shape, or doubles 6 instead of adding 1

quiz.q: A 4×4 grid is made of small squares. How many of the smallest squares are there?
quiz.explain: 4 rows with 4 squares in each row make 4 × 4 = 16 small squares.
quiz.mistake: Adds 4 + 4, or counts only the squares around the border (12)

quiz.q: Kabir joins every pair of 5 dots with a straight line. How many lines does he draw?
quiz.explain: The 1st dot joins 4 others, the 2nd joins 3 new ones, then 2, then 1: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Counts each line twice (20) or thinks one line per dot (5)

quiz.q: The Koch snowflake starts with 3 lines. Each step turns every line into 4 smaller lines. How many lines are there after 2 steps?
quiz.explain: After step 1: 3 × 4 = 12 lines. After step 2: 12 × 4 = 48 lines.
quiz.mistake: Adds 4 lines each step, or stops after 1 step (12)

quiz.q: In a Diwali rangoli, the rows have 1, 3, 5, 7, ... diyas. How many diyas are in the 6th row?
quiz.explain: Each row has 2 more diyas: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The 6th row has 11.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the 6th row has 2 × 6 = 12, or stops at row 5

quiz.q: Square grids 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, ... have 1, 4, 9, ... small squares. Which grid has 49 small squares?
quiz.explain: 7 × 7 = 49, so the 7 × 7 grid has 49 small squares.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a nearby grid without multiplying

quiz.q: Which picture pattern gives the numbers 1, 3, 6, 10?
options: Sides of a triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon
Lines joining every pair of 2, 3, 4, 5 dots
Lines in the first four Koch snowflake steps
quiz.explain: 2, 3, 4 and 5 dots need 1, 3, 6 and 10 lines. The others give 3, 4, 5, 6 and 1, 4, 9, 16 and 3, 12, 48, 192.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up triangular numbers with square numbers or counting numbers

quiz.q: How many corners does a regular octagon have?
quiz.explain: Octa means eight. An octagon has 8 sides, and every polygon has as many corners as sides.
quiz.mistake: Confuses octagon with hexagon (6) or decagon (10)

teach.ask: Gappu is staring at a rangoli: 'How can a picture pattern turn into a number pattern?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Count the same thing in each picture and the numbers make a pattern. Lovely!
teach.nudge: What exactly should I count in each picture, and how does it change from one picture to the next?

learn.hook: Stack laddoos in a triangle or a square and you discover two of the most famous number families!
points: Triangular numbers count dots arranged in a triangle: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, ... The 5th one is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
Square numbers count dots arranged in a square: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... The 5th one is 5 × 5 = 25.
Adding odd numbers from 1 gives square numbers: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4 × 4.
Two triangular numbers next to each other add up to a square: 6 + 10 = 16.
Counting up and back down gives a square too: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9 = 3 × 3.

example.q: Find the 7th triangular number.

learn.reallife: Bowling pins and a carrom board's starting coins sit in triangles; chessboards and tiled floors show square numbers.

quiz.q: What is the 6th triangular number?
quiz.mistake: Gives the 5th triangular number (15) or the 6th square number (36)

quiz.q: What is the 8th square number?
quiz.explain: The 8th square number is 8 × 8 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 + 8 = 16 instead of multiplying 8 × 8

quiz.q: Aisha arranges laddoos in a square tray with 9 rows and 9 laddoos in each row. How many laddoos are there?
quiz.explain: 9 rows of 9 is 9 × 9 = 81 laddoos, a square number.
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 + 9 instead of multiplying, or makes a times-table slip (72, 90)

quiz.explain: These are the first 6 odd numbers, and their sum is 6 × 6 = 36.
steps: Count the odd numbers: 6 of them
quiz.mistake: Forgets the last number (25) or makes an adding slip

quiz.q: Which two neighbouring triangular numbers add up to 25?
quiz.explain: 10 and 15 are next to each other in 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, and 10 + 15 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Picks 9 and 16, which add to 25 but are square numbers, not triangular ones

quiz.q: Harpreet stacks cricket balls in a triangle: 1 ball in the top row, 2 in the next, then 3, with 5 rows in all. How many balls does he use?
quiz.explain: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, the 5th triangular number.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 4 rows (10) or uses the square number 5 × 5 = 25

quiz.explain: Counting up to 5 and back down to 1 gives 5 × 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Counts the 5 twice (30) or only adds one side (15)

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is BOTH a triangular number and a square number?
quiz.explain: 36 = 6 × 6 is square, and 36 = 1 + 2 + ... + 8 is the 8th triangular number. 16 and 25 are only square; 10 is only triangular.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one of the two lists

teach.ask: Gappu has a pile of laddoos: 'What is the difference between a triangular number and a square number?'
teach.praise: Wow! Triangles grow by adding 1, 2, 3, ... and squares are a number times itself. I'll stack my laddoos both ways!
teach.nudge: How do I actually work out a triangular number? And a square one?

learn.hook: Every drawing in geometry is built from tiny dots and straight paths. Let's meet the building blocks!
points: A point marks an exact spot. We name it with a capital letter, like point P.
A line segment is the straight path between two points. It has two endpoints and a length we can measure, like segment AB.
A line goes on forever in both directions. Through two points, exactly one line can pass.
A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. Ray OA starts at O and passes through A.
An angle is made by two rays that start from the same point. That point is the vertex, and the rays are the arms.

example.q: A figure starts at point O, passes through point A and goes on forever. Name it.
steps: It has one starting point (O) and no end.
A figure with one endpoint that goes on forever is a ray.
We write the starting point first.

learn.reallife: A torch beam is like a ray, the edge of your ruler is a line segment, and the tip of a pencil marks a point.

games.title: Match the real thing to the geometry word
pairs: A straight path with no ends at all
Two arms of an open pair of scissors

games.title: True or false?
items: A line segment has two endpoints.
It starts at one point and stops at another.
A ray has two endpoints.
A ray has only one endpoint; it goes on forever the other way.
Exactly one line can pass through two given points.
Two points fix one straight line.
We can measure the length of a line with a ruler.
A line goes on forever. Only a line segment has a length.
Ray PQ and ray QP are the same ray.
Ray PQ starts at P, ray QP starts at Q. They point in opposite directions.
Many lines can pass through a single point.
You can draw lines through one point in every direction.

quiz.q: How many endpoints does a line segment have?
quiz.explain: A line segment starts at one point and ends at another, so it has 2 endpoints.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up a segment with a ray (1 endpoint) or a line (0 endpoints)

quiz.q: Which figure starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction?
quiz.explain: A ray has one starting point and no end in the other direction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a line has a starting point

quiz.q: In ray XY, which point is the starting point?
quiz.explain: A ray is always named starting point first, so ray XY starts at X and passes through Y.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the first letter names the starting point of a ray

quiz.q: Points A, B and C lie on one straight line in that order. How many different line segments can you name using these points?
quiz.explain: The segments are AB, BC and AC. AB and BA are the same segment, so there are 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the long segment AC (2), or counts AB and BA as different (6)

quiz.q: How many straight lines can pass through two different points P and Q?
quiz.explain: Two points fix exactly one straight line.
quiz.mistake: Thinks of curved paths, which are not straight lines

quiz.q: An angle is made by...
options: two rays with the same starting point
quiz.explain: Two rays starting from one point (the vertex) form an angle. The rays are its arms.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the arms of an angle must meet at a vertex

quiz.q: Joseph marks 4 points, with no three on one straight line, and joins every pair. How many line segments does he draw?
quiz.explain: The first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, then 1: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts each segment twice (12) or draws only the outline (4)

quiz.q: Which of these can be measured with a ruler?
quiz.explain: Only a line segment has two ends, so only it has a fixed length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a line or ray has a fixed length

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'A line, a ray and a line segment all look straight! How are they different?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Segment: two ends. Ray: one end, goes on one way. Line: no ends, goes on both ways. Got it!
teach.nudge: But how many ends does each one have, and which way does it keep going?

learn.hook: How much does a door open? How far do clock hands turn? Degrees tell us exactly!
points: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between its arms. We measure it in degrees (°).
A full turn is 360°, a half turn (straight angle) is 180° and a quarter turn (right angle) is 90°.
Using a protractor: put its centre on the vertex, line up the baseline with one arm, and read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm.
Longer or shorter arms do not change the angle. Only the opening matters.
On a clock, the hour marks are 360° ÷ 12 = 30° apart.

example.q: What is the smaller angle between the clock hands at 4 o'clock?
steps: At 4:00 the hands are 4 gaps apart

learn.reallife: A cricket coach talks about the angle of the bat, and a fan blade or a door hinge turns through angles.

games.title: Smallest turn to biggest turn
games.prompt: Put these angles from smallest to largest
items: A quarter turn
A straight angle
Three quarter turns
A full turn

quiz.q: How many degrees are there in a quarter turn?
quiz.explain: A full turn is 360°, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
quiz.mistake: Halves twice wrongly (45°) or thinks of a half turn (180°)

quiz.q: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at 2:00?
quiz.explain: The hands are 2 hour-gaps apart and each gap is 30°, so 2 × 30° = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one gap (30°) or thinks each hour is 10° (20°)

quiz.q: Kabir faces North and turns clockwise until he faces South. How many degrees does he turn?
quiz.explain: North to South is a half turn, which is 180°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one quarter turn reaches South (90°) or uses a full turn (360°)

quiz.q: Meena puts a protractor on angle PQR. Arm QP is on 0 of the inner scale. Arm QR crosses 50 on the inner scale and 130 on the outer scale. What is the angle?
quiz.explain: Read the same scale that starts at 0 on the first arm. That is the inner scale, which shows 50°.
steps: Arm QP sits on 0 of the inner scale
Use the inner scale for arm QR: 50
quiz.mistake: Reads the outer scale, which starts at 180 on that arm

quiz.q: Arjun draws a 40° angle with arms 3 cm long. Riya draws a 40° angle with arms 10 cm long. Which angle is bigger?
quiz.explain: Both angles measure 40°. Longer arms do not make the opening bigger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks longer arms make a bigger angle

quiz.q: A fielder spins round three quarters of a full turn. How many degrees is that?
quiz.explain: One quarter turn is 90°, so three quarters is 3 × 90° = 270°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 3 × 100 or a half turn instead of three quarters

quiz.q: What is the smaller angle between the clock hands at 5:00?
quiz.explain: The hands are 5 hour-gaps apart: 5 × 30° = 150°. The other way round is 210°, which is the bigger angle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each hour is 10° (50°) or gives the bigger angle (210°)

quiz.q: Angle AOB = 35° and angle BOC = 50°. They sit side by side, sharing arm OB. What is angle AOC?
quiz.explain: Angles side by side add up: 35° + 50° = 85°.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the angles (15°) or makes an adding slip

teach.ask: Gappu holds a protractor upside down: 'How do I measure how big an angle is?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Centre on the vertex, one arm on zero, read the degrees. I measured my wing angle!
teach.nudge: Where do I put the protractor, and which zero do I start reading from?

learn.hook: Angles have names, just like cricket shots! Sharp, square, wide and more.
points: An acute angle is more than 0° but less than 90°, like the tip of a pizza slice.
A right angle is exactly 90°, like the corner of a book. It is marked with a small square.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°.
A straight angle is exactly 180°. A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°.
Two lines that meet at a right angle are called perpendicular lines.

example.q: What type of angle is 135°?

learn.reallife: The corner of a door is a right angle, an open laptop screen usually makes an obtuse angle, and scissors open a little make an acute angle.

games.title: Acute, right or obtuse?
items: Clock hands at 1:00
Corner of a notebook
Clock hands at 9:00
Clock hands at 5:00

games.title: Angle facts
items: An angle of 90° is an acute angle.
90° is exactly a right angle. Acute angles are less than 90°.
Every obtuse angle is bigger than every acute angle.
Obtuse angles are more than 90° and acute angles are less than 90°.
A straight angle measures 180°.
A straight angle is a half turn.
Two acute angles always add up to an obtuse angle.
20° + 30° = 50°, which is still acute.
The clock hands at 3:00 make a right angle.
3 hour-gaps × 30° = 90°.
A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°.
That is the meaning of reflex.

quiz.q: What type of angle is 72°?
quiz.explain: 72° is less than 90°, so it is acute.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the meanings of acute and obtuse

quiz.q: What type of angle is 145°?
quiz.explain: 145° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any angle over 90° is reflex

quiz.q: The hands of a clock at 3:00 make which type of angle?
quiz.explain: At 3:00 the hands are 3 × 30° = 90° apart, which is a right angle.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the picture without working out the degrees

quiz.q: Aisha opens a book flat on the table so its two covers lie in one straight line. What angle do the covers make?
quiz.explain: Covers lying in one straight line make a straight angle of 180°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a flat, open book makes a right angle

quiz.q: Which of these is a reflex angle?
quiz.explain: A reflex angle is between 180° and 360°. Only 250° fits.
quiz.mistake: Picks 170°, which is obtuse because it is less than 180°

quiz.q: Two lines cross so that all four angles are right angles. What are these lines called?
quiz.explain: Lines that meet at right angles are perpendicular. Parallel lines never meet at all.
quiz.mistake: Confuses perpendicular with parallel

quiz.q: Joseph says the smaller angle between the clock hands at 10:00 is obtuse. Is he right?
options: No, it is a right angle
No, it is 60°, an acute angle
quiz.explain: From 10 to 12 is 2 hour-gaps: 2 × 30° = 60°, which is acute.
quiz.mistake: Counts the gaps the long way round or miscounts

quiz.q: An angle is split into two equal parts of 50° each. What type is the whole angle?
quiz.explain: The whole angle is 50° + 50° = 100°, which is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Looks at one part (50°, acute) instead of the whole angle

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'Acute, right, obtuse, straight... how do I tell which is which?'
teach.praise: Yay! Less than 90° is acute, exactly 90° is right, between 90° and 180° is obtuse, 180° is straight. I'm an angle expert!
teach.nudge: What number do I compare the angle with to decide its type?

learn.hook: Numbers have personalities! Some are even, some are odd, some are 'supercells' that tower over their neighbours.
points: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, and even + odd = odd.
The digit sum of a number is what you get when you add its digits: for 347 it is 3 + 4 + 7 = 14.
In a row of numbers, a supercell is a number bigger than all its neighbours. A number at either end has only one neighbour.
Collatz game: if a number is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Every number anyone has tried so far ends at 1.

example.q: Play the Collatz game starting with 6.

learn.reallife: Pairing up children for a game works only when the number is even; shopkeepers quickly check bills using digit sums.

games.title: Will the answer be even or odd?

items.text: The digit sum of 4352 is ___
The smallest 3-digit number with digit sum 5 is ___
Odd + odd always gives an ___ number.
In the row 4, 9, 2, 7, 3 the supercells are 9 and ___

quiz.q: Is the sum 37 + 48 + 15 even or odd?
quiz.explain: Odd + even + odd: the two odd numbers make an even, and even + even is even. The total is 100.
quiz.mistake: Thinks that adding any odd number makes the answer odd

quiz.q: What is the digit sum of 9078?
quiz.mistake: Skips a digit or makes an adding slip

quiz.q: How many supercells are in this row: 5, 8, 3, 6, 1, 4? (A supercell is bigger than all its neighbours.)
quiz.explain: 8 is bigger than 5 and 3; 6 is bigger than 3 and 1; 4 at the end has only one neighbour, 1, and is bigger. So there are 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a number at the end has only one neighbour

quiz.q: Start the Collatz game at 5 (even → halve, odd → × 3 + 1). What is the third number after 5?
quiz.explain: 5 → 16 → 8 → 4. The third number after 5 is 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts 5 itself as a step, or stops too early

quiz.q: Arjun adds five odd numbers. The answer must be...
quiz.explain: Four odd numbers make two even pairs, and the fifth odd number makes the total odd. For example 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding odd numbers always gives an even answer

quiz.q: Which of these numbers has digits that add up to 10?
quiz.mistake: Adds only the first two digits

quiz.q: Meena says: 'Adding two even numbers always gives an even number.' Is she right?
quiz.explain: Each even number is made of pairs. Putting pairs together still gives only pairs, so the sum is even.
quiz.mistake: Thinks large even numbers might behave differently

quiz.q: Kabir looks at the numbers from 1 to 20. How many of them have a digit sum of 5?
quiz.explain: Only 5 and 14 (1 + 4 = 5) have a digit sum of 5 between 1 and 20.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the single-digit number 5, or includes 23 which is bigger than 20

teach.ask: Gappu has 7 + 9 written in the sand: 'Without adding, can you tell if the answer is even or odd? How?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Odd + odd makes even because the two leftover ones pair up. Clever!
teach.nudge: Why does odd + odd turn out even? What happens to the leftovers?

learn.hook: MALAYALAM reads the same backwards! Numbers can play this mirror game too.
points: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards: 121, 4334, 7 and the word MALAYALAM.
Every 1-digit number is a palindrome. A 3-digit palindrome has the same first and last digit, like 505.
Reverse-and-add: add a number to its reverse, then repeat with the answer until you get a palindrome.
Example: 39 + 93 = 132, then 132 + 231 = 363, a palindrome.
Clocks show palindrome times too, like 12:21 and 10:01.

example.q: Do reverse-and-add on 57 until you get a palindrome.

learn.reallife: Look for palindrome bus numbers, car number plates and dates like 22-02-2022!

items.text: The palindrome between 140 and 150 is ___
The largest 3-digit palindrome is ___

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is a palindrome?
quiz.explain: 2442 backwards is 2442. The others change when reversed, for example 2424 becomes 4242.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number with repeating digits is always a palindrome

quiz.q: How many 2-digit palindromes are there?
quiz.explain: They are 11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99, which makes 9. (00 is not a 2-digit number.)
steps: Both digits must be the same
quiz.mistake: Counts 00 as a 2-digit number

quiz.q: Do reverse-and-add on 48: 48 + 84 = 132. Then 132 + 231 = ?
quiz.explain: 132 + 231 = 363, which is a palindrome.
quiz.mistake: Doubles 132 instead of adding its reverse (264)

quiz.q: Riya's digital clock shows 10:01. Is it a palindrome time?
options: Yes, 1001 reads the same both ways
quiz.explain: Ignoring the colon, the digits 1-0-0-1 read the same forwards and backwards.
quiz.mistake: Compares the two halves without reversing the second one

quiz.q: What is the smallest 3-digit palindrome?
quiz.explain: The first digit must be 1 and the last digit must match it, so the smallest is 1_1 with 0 in the middle: 101.
quiz.mistake: Chooses 100, which reads 001 backwards

quiz.q: Which of these state languages is spelled as a palindrome in English capital letters?
quiz.explain: MALAYALAM backwards is M-A-L-A-Y-A-L-A-M, exactly the same.
quiz.mistake: Checks only the first and last letters

quiz.q: How many 3-digit palindromes start with the digit 5?
quiz.explain: They look like 5_5, and the middle digit can be any of 0 to 9: 505, 515, ..., 595. That is 10.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the middle digit can be 0

quiz.q: Reverse-and-add on 23 gives a palindrome after how many steps?
quiz.explain: 23 + 32 = 55, which is already a palindrome. So it takes just 1 step.
quiz.mistake: Keeps adding after a palindrome has already appeared

teach.ask: Gappu writes 1221 in the sand: 'Someone called this a palindrome. What does that mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It reads the same forwards and backwards, like MALAYALAM. I'll spot them on number plates!
teach.nudge: What happens when you read it from the other end?

learn.hook: Pick almost any 4-digit number, follow a simple recipe, and you will always land on 6174. Spooky? No, it's maths!
points: Take a 4-digit number whose digits are not all the same.
Arrange its digits from largest to smallest, and again from smallest to largest.
Subtract the smaller number from the larger one. Keep zeros: 0378 counts as a 4-digit arrangement.
Repeat with the answer. You always reach 6174 within 7 steps, and 7641 − 1467 = 6174 brings it back to itself.
This was discovered by D. R. Kaprekar, a maths teacher from Maharashtra. For 3-digit numbers the routine ends at 495.

example.q: Run Kaprekar's routine on 3524.

learn.reallife: It's a great party trick: ask a friend for a 4-digit number and tell them where they'll end up before they start!

games.title: Kaprekar's recipe
games.prompt: Put the steps in the right order
items: Pick a 4-digit number whose digits are not all the same
Arrange its digits to make the largest and the smallest numbers
Subtract the smaller number from the larger
Repeat with the answer until you reach 6174

quiz.q: What is Kaprekar's constant for 4-digit numbers?
quiz.explain: Every 4-digit number (digits not all the same) reaches 6174, and 7641 − 1467 = 6174 again.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the arranged numbers, or the 3-digit constant 495

quiz.q: Start with 2005. Arrange its digits largest-first and smallest-first, then subtract. What do you get?
quiz.explain: Largest: 5200. Smallest: 0025, which is 25. 5200 − 25 = 5175.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the original number (3195), keeps only one zero in front (4995) or adds (5225)

quiz.q: Joseph uses 6174 in Kaprekar's routine. What does he get next?
quiz.explain: Largest 7641 − smallest 1467 = 6174. It comes back to itself, so the routine stops there.
quiz.mistake: Stops after arranging the digits instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Why can't we use 3333 in Kaprekar's routine?
options: All its digits are the same, so the answer is 0 at once
quiz.explain: 3333 − 3333 = 0, so the routine gets stuck. Other palindromes like 4224 work fine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks palindromes cannot be used

quiz.q: For 3-digit numbers (digits not all the same), Kaprekar's routine ends at which number?
quiz.explain: For 3 digits the routine ends at 495, because 954 − 459 = 495.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 4-digit constant or reverses the digits (594)

quiz.q: Aisha starts with 4321. What is the first subtraction answer?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to borrow (3097 or 3187), or adds instead (5555)

quiz.q: Next step from 3087: the arrangements are 8730 and 0378. What is 8730 − 378?
quiz.mistake: Makes a borrowing slip, or adds instead of subtracting (9108)

quiz.q: Who discovered the special property of 6174?
options: D. R. Kaprekar, a maths teacher from Maharashtra
quiz.explain: D. R. Kaprekar found this routine, which is why 6174 is called Kaprekar's constant.
quiz.mistake: Guesses another famous Indian mathematician

teach.ask: Gappu has the number 2196: 'Show me the Kaprekar trick! What do I do?'
teach.praise: Wow! Biggest minus smallest, again and again, and I reached 6174. Magic maths!
teach.nudge: After arranging the digits two ways, what do I do with those two numbers?

learn.hook: Which sweet does your class love most? Don't guess. Collect the data and find out!
points: Data is a collection of facts, like numbers or names, gathered to answer a question.
Tally marks help us count as we collect: draw one stroke for each item, and make the fifth stroke cross the first four to make a bundle of 5.
A frequency table lists each item and how many times it appears (its frequency).
Arranging data in order, from smallest to largest, makes it easy to find the biggest and smallest values.
Check your total: the frequencies should add up to the number of things you counted.

example.q: Arjun asked 15 friends their favourite fruit: mango 7, banana 3, apple 5. Make tally marks and find the favourite.
steps: Mango: one bundle of 5 and 2 strokes = 7
example.answer: Mango is the favourite, chosen by 7 friends.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers count which items sell most before Diwali, and cricket scorers keep data on every ball bowled.

games.title: Match the tally to the number
Data detectives
items: In tally marks, the fifth stroke is drawn across the first four.
This makes bundles of 5 that are easy to count.
A frequency table shows how many times each item appears.
Frequency means 'how many times'.
Data can only be numbers, never words like 'mango'.
Names, colours and choices are data too.
A bundle of 5 and 2 more strokes stand for 7.
Sorting data from smallest to largest makes it harder to find the biggest value.
After sorting, the biggest value is simply at the end.

quiz.q: A tally shows 3 bundles of five and 2 single strokes. What number is this?
quiz.explain: Each bundle is 5, so 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
quiz.mistake: Writes the 3 and the 2 side by side (32) or forgets the single strokes

quiz.q: Meena asked her class how they come to school: Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3. How many children did she ask?
quiz.explain: Add all the frequencies: 12 + 8 + 5 + 3 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Forgets one group, or counts the number of groups (4)

items: Bus
Walk
Cycle
Car

quiz.q: Using Meena's data (Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3), how many more children come by bus than by cycle?
quiz.explain: 'How many more' means subtract: 12 − 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two numbers (17) instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: How do you show 14 using tally marks?
quiz.explain: 14 = 5 + 5 + 4, so it is 2 bundles of five and 4 single strokes.
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits 1 and 4 as 1 bundle and 4 strokes (which is only 9)

quiz.q: Scores in 6 cricket matches: 45, 12, 67, 30, 89, 54. Arrange them from smallest to largest. Which score is third?
quiz.explain: In order: 12, 30, 45, 54, 67, 89. The third score is 45.
quiz.mistake: Picks the third score from the unsorted list (67)

quiz.q: At a Makar Sankranti fair, Kabir counts 20 kites: red 6, yellow 4, green 3 and the rest blue. How many kites are blue?
quiz.explain: Red, yellow and green make 6 + 4 + 3 = 13. The rest: 20 − 13 = 7 blue kites.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total of the other colours (13) instead of what is left

quiz.q: What is the best way to find out the favourite sweet of the students in your class?
options: Ask every student and record the answers with tally marks
Count the sweets in a shop
quiz.explain: To answer a question about the class, collect data from everyone in the class and record it carefully.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one person's choice tells us about the whole class

quiz.q: In a frequency table of favourite colours, what does 'frequency' mean?
options: How many times each colour was chosen
The largest number in the table
The name of the person who chose it
quiz.explain: Frequency tells us how many times something appears in the data.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the item with how often it appears

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know which fruit all the birds like most: 'How do I collect and count everyone's answer?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Ask everyone, tally as I go, then make a table. Now I know it's guava!
teach.nudge: Once I have everyone's answers, how do I keep count without getting muddled?

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! Graphs let you see data at a glance.
points: A pictograph shows data with pictures. A key tells what one picture stands for, like 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes.
Half a picture stands for half the key value.
A bar graph uses bars of the same width with equal gaps. The length of each bar shows the value.
A scale such as 1 unit = 10 children lets big numbers fit on the page. Choose a scale that keeps bars a sensible size.
Every graph needs a title and labels on both axes so readers know what it shows.

example.q: Key: 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes. A row shows 5 whole 🥭 and half a 🥭. How many mangoes?

learn.reallife: Newspapers show cricket run rates and rainfall with bar graphs, and school notice boards use pictographs for attendance.

items.text: Key: 1 🏏 = 2 matches. Six 🏏 show ___ matches.
Key: 1 🍦 = 5 ice creams. 35 ice creams need ___ pictures.
Scale: 1 unit = 10 km. A bar 4 units long shows ___ km.
In a bar graph, all bars should have the same ___.

quiz.q: In a pictograph, 1 🍪 = 10 cookies. Riya's row shows 4 🍪. How many cookies did she bake?
quiz.explain: Each picture means 10 cookies, so 4 pictures mean 4 × 10 = 40.
quiz.mistake: Counts the pictures without using the key (4) or adds 4 + 10

quiz.q: Key: 1 🚂 = 100 passengers. How many 🚂 pictures show 350 passengers?
quiz.explain: 300 passengers need 3 pictures and the extra 50 is half of 100, so half a picture: 3 and a half.
quiz.mistake: Drops the extra 50 (3) or rounds up (4)

quiz.q: A sweet shop sold laddoos in Diwali week: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40. On which day were the most laddoos sold?
quiz.explain: 40 is the largest value, so Thursday has the longest bar.
quiz.mistake: Picks the second-longest bar

items: Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu

quiz.q: Using the same laddoo data (Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40), how many laddoos were sold on Monday and Wednesday together?
quiz.explain: Monday 20 + Wednesday 15 = 35 laddoos.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding (5)

quiz.q: Aisha's bar graph uses the scale 1 unit = 5 students. The bar for Kabaddi is 6 units long. How many students chose Kabaddi?
quiz.explain: Each unit stands for 5 students, so 6 units stand for 6 × 5 = 30 students.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bar length without the scale (6) or adds 6 + 5

quiz.q: Four baskets hold 120, 80, 200 and 150 mangoes. Which scale is best for a bar graph in your notebook?
quiz.explain: With 1 unit = 20, the bars are 6, 4, 10 and 7.5 units long: they fit and are easy to draw. 1 mango per unit makes bars far too long; 1000 makes them tiny; 7 gives awkward numbers.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about whether the bars will fit on the page

quiz.q: Key: 1 🌳 = 8 trees. How many trees does half a 🌳 show?
quiz.explain: Half of 8 is 4.
quiz.mistake: Treats half a picture as a whole picture (8) or doubles it (16)

quiz.q: Joseph's bar graph shows that Class 6A read 32 books and Class 6B read 24 books. How many more books did 6A read?
quiz.explain: 32 − 24 = 8 more books.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values (56) instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu sees a pictograph of mangoes: 'There are only 3 mango pictures. Does that mean 3 mangoes?'
teach.praise: Chirp! I must read the key first. If 1 picture means 10 mangoes, 3 pictures mean 30!
teach.nudge: Is there something on the graph that tells me what one picture is worth?

learn.hook: Idli for 3, vada for 5, idli-vada for both! Let's play a game that hides factors and multiples.
points: A factor of a number divides it exactly, with no remainder. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
A multiple of a number is in its times table. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, ...
1 is a factor of every number, and every number is a factor and a multiple of itself.
Common multiples belong to two times tables. In the idli-vada game, say 'idli' for multiples of 3, 'vada' for multiples of 5 and 'idli-vada' for multiples of both, like 15 and 30.
A perfect number equals the sum of its factors other than itself: 6 = 1 + 2 + 3.

example.q: Find the common factors of 18 and 24.

learn.reallife: Packing 24 laddoos into equal boxes uses factors; buses that leave every 10 and every 15 minutes meet again at common multiples.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a factor of 36?
quiz.explain: 36 ÷ 8 = 4 remainder 4, so 8 is not a factor. 36 = 9 × 4 and 36 = 12 × 3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every even number below 36 is a factor of 36

quiz.q: How many factors does 20 have?
quiz.explain: Factor pairs of 20: 1 × 20, 2 × 10, 4 × 5. That gives 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, which is 6 factors.
quiz.mistake: Forgets 1 or the number itself

quiz.q: In the idli-vada game (idli for multiples of 3, vada for multiples of 5, idli-vada for both), which is the first number where Riya says 'idli-vada'?
quiz.explain: The first number in both the 3 and 5 times tables is 15.
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 + 5 = 8 instead of finding a common multiple

quiz.q: Which number is a common multiple of 6 and 8?
quiz.explain: 24 = 6 × 4 and 24 = 8 × 3. 36 is not in the 8 table, and 32 is not in the 6 table.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one of the two times tables

quiz.q: Laddoos can be packed in boxes of 4 or boxes of 6. What is the smallest number of laddoos that fills boxes of 4 exactly AND boxes of 6 exactly?
quiz.explain: We need the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6, which is 12.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 4 × 6 = 24 (common, but not the smallest) or adds them

quiz.q: What is the greatest common factor of 16 and 40?
quiz.explain: Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Factors of 40: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 40. The biggest one in both is 8.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a smaller common factor (4), or picks 16, which does not divide 40

quiz.q: 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 makes 6 a 'perfect number'. Which of these is also a perfect number?
quiz.explain: The factors of 28 other than itself are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, and 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without adding the factors

quiz.q: Arjun says 1 is a factor of every number. Is he right?
options: Yes, any number divided by 1 leaves no remainder
No, 1 is a multiple, not a factor
quiz.explain: Every number n = 1 × n, so 1 divides every number exactly.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1 always divides exactly

teach.ask: Gappu has 12 seeds: 'What's the difference between a factor of 12 and a multiple of 12?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Factors divide 12 exactly, like 3 and 4. Multiples are in 12's times table, like 24 and 36!
teach.nudge: Which ones divide 12, and which ones come from the 12 times table?

learn.hook: Prime numbers are the building blocks of all numbers, like atoms are for everything around us!
points: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.
A composite number has more than two factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10.
1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7, ... and the numbers left are prime.
Every composite number can be written as a product of primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Two numbers are co-prime if their only common factor is 1, like 8 and 15.

example.q: Write 60 as a product of primes.

learn.reallife: Prime numbers keep your online payments and phone messages safe, because big numbers are hard to break into primes.

games.title: Prime facts
items: 2 is the only even prime number.
Every other even number has 2 as an extra factor.
1 is a prime number.
1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
Every odd number is prime.
9 is odd but 9 = 3 × 3.
8 and 15 are co-prime.
Their only common factor is 1.
A composite number has more than two factors.
That is what composite means.
18 = 2 × 3 × 3 as a product of primes.
2 × 3 × 3 = 18 and 2 and 3 are prime.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prime number?
quiz.explain: 37 has only the factors 1 and 37. 39 = 3 × 13, 49 = 7 × 7 and 27 = 3 × 9.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every odd number is prime

quiz.q: How many prime numbers are there between 10 and 20?
quiz.explain: The primes are 11, 13, 17 and 19. That is 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts 15 as prime because it is odd

quiz.q: Why is 1 not a prime number?
quiz.explain: A prime must have exactly two factors. 1 has only one factor, itself.
quiz.mistake: Thinks size or oddness decides whether a number is prime

quiz.q: Write 36 as a product of primes.
quiz.explain: 36 = 2 × 18 = 2 × 2 × 9 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Only the last form uses primes alone.
quiz.mistake: Stops early with composite factors like 4, 6, 9 or 18

quiz.q: Which pair of numbers is co-prime?
quiz.explain: 9 = 3 × 3 and 16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 share no factor except 1. The others share 6, 5 and 7.
quiz.mistake: Thinks numbers must be prime to be co-prime

quiz.q: Kabir says 91 is prime. Is he right?
options: Yes, because it does not end in 5
quiz.explain: 7 × 13 = 91, so 91 has factors other than 1 and itself. (9 × 11 = 99, not 91.)
quiz.mistake: Checks only 2, 3 and 5 and forgets to try 7

quiz.q: What is the smallest composite number?
quiz.explain: 4 has factors 1, 2, 4 (more than two). 1 is neither, and 2 and 3 are prime.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 1 or 2 is composite

quiz.q: A number's prime factorisation is 2 × 3 × 7. What is the number?
quiz.mistake: Writes the digits side by side (237) or adds them (12)

teach.ask: Gappu counts pebbles: 'My friend says 7 is prime but 8 is composite. What do those words mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Prime means only 1 and itself as factors. Composite has more. And 1 is neither!
teach.nudge: How many factors does a prime number have? And a composite one?

learn.hook: Can 7452 sweets be shared equally among 4 friends? You can tell in 2 seconds without dividing!
points: By 2: the last digit is even. By 5: the last digit is 0 or 5. By 10: the last digit is 0.
By 3: the digit sum is divisible by 3. By 9: the digit sum is divisible by 9.
By 4: the number formed by the last two digits is divisible by 4.
By 8: the number formed by the last three digits is divisible by 8.
By 6: the number is divisible by both 2 and 3.

example.q: Is 7452 divisible by 4? By 9?
steps: Last two digits: 52, and 52 ÷ 4 = 13, so yes for 4
18 is divisible by 9, so yes for 9
example.answer: Yes, it is divisible by both 4 and 9.

learn.reallife: Teachers use divisibility to split a class into equal teams, and shopkeepers to pack items in equal boxes.

games.title: Match the clue to the rule

quiz.q: Which number is divisible by 9?
quiz.explain: 4 + 5 + 3 + 6 = 18, which is divisible by 9. The others have digit sums 19, 13 and 11.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the last digit instead of the digit sum

quiz.q: Is 3416 divisible by 8?
options: No, because its digit sum 14 is not a multiple of 8
quiz.explain: For 8, check the last three digits: 416 = 8 × 52, so 3416 is divisible by 8.
quiz.mistake: Uses the digit-sum rule, which only works for 3 and 9

quiz.q: Meena has 234 marbles. Can she share them equally among 6 friends?
options: No, there will be 4 left over
quiz.explain: 234 is even and its digit sum 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 is divisible by 3, so it is divisible by 6. 234 ÷ 6 = 39.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one of the two rules for 6, or makes a division slip

quiz.q: Which digit in the blank makes 52_ divisible by both 2 and 5?
quiz.explain: To be divisible by 2 and 5, a number must end in 0. So the number is 520.
quiz.mistake: Picks 5, which works for 5 but makes the number odd

quiz.q: Which number is divisible by 4?
quiz.explain: The last two digits of 1732 are 32, and 32 = 4 × 8. 34, 26 and 50 are not multiples of 4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every even number is divisible by 4

quiz.q: The number 7_2 is divisible by 3. Which digit could go in the blank?
quiz.explain: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12, which is divisible by 3. With 1, 2 or 4 the digit sums are 10, 11 and 13.
quiz.mistake: Checks only the last digit

quiz.q: Harpreet looks at 108000. Which fact shows quickly that it is divisible by 10?
quiz.explain: A number is divisible by 10 when its last digit is 0. Being even is not enough (for example 12).
quiz.mistake: Thinks being even is enough for 10

quiz.q: Is 2346 divisible by 6?
options: No, because its digit sum 15 is not a multiple of 6
No, because it is not divisible by 9
No, because 46 is not a multiple of 6
Yes, because it is even and its digit sum 15 is a multiple of 3
quiz.explain: For 6, the number must pass the tests for 2 and 3. 2346 is even and 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15 is a multiple of 3. (2346 ÷ 6 = 391.)
quiz.mistake: Applies the digit sum to 6 directly, or uses a last-two-digits rule that only works for 4

teach.ask: Gappu has 135 grains: 'How can I tell if they share equally among 3, 5 or 9 birds without dividing?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 135 ends in 5, so 5 works. Digits add to 9, so 3 and 9 work too. Shortcuts are fun!
teach.nudge: Which part of the number do I look at for 5, and what do I do with the digits for 3 and 9?

learn.hook: How much lace goes around a dupatta? How long is the boundary rope of a cricket ground? That's perimeter!
points: Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary of a shape. Add the lengths of all the sides.
Rectangle: perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth).
Square: perimeter = 4 × side.
Regular polygon (all sides equal): perimeter = number of sides × side length. An equilateral triangle is 3 × side.
Perimeter is a length, so it uses units like cm or m.

example.q: A garden is 12 m long and 8 m wide. How much fencing goes all round it?

learn.reallife: Framing a photo, putting lights around a window for Diwali and running laps of a ground all use perimeter.

items.q: Side of a square with perimeter 36 cm
Triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm

games.title: Match the shape to its perimeter

quiz.q: Riya's rangoli is a square of side 15 cm. She sticks ribbon all around its edge. How much ribbon does she need?
quiz.explain: A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 × 15 = 60 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies side × side (area, 225) or uses only 2 or 3 sides

quiz.q: The boundary rope of a school cricket ground goes around a rectangle 70 m long and 50 m wide. How long is the rope?
quiz.mistake: Adds length and breadth only once (120) or multiplies them (area)

quiz.q: Arjun walks 3 times around a triangular park with sides 30 m, 40 m and 50 m. How far does he walk?
quiz.explain: One round is 30 + 40 + 50 = 120 m. Three rounds are 3 × 120 = 360 m.
quiz.mistake: Gives the distance for only one round (120 m)

quiz.q: The perimeter of a square is 48 cm. How long is one side?
quiz.explain: A square has 4 equal sides, so one side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 4 (24) or multiplies (192)

quiz.q: A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and length 10 cm. What is its breadth?
quiz.explain: Half the perimeter is length + breadth = 15 cm. So breadth = 15 − 10 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 10 from 30 without halving first (20)

quiz.q: A regular hexagon tile has each side 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: A hexagon has 6 equal sides: 6 × 8 = 48 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong number of sides (5, 7 or 8)

quiz.q: Which has the bigger perimeter: a square of side 6 cm or a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm?
quiz.explain: Square: 4 × 6 = 24 cm. Rectangle: 2 × (8 + 3) = 22 cm. The square is bigger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape with the longest side must have the bigger perimeter

quiz.q: Fencing costs ₹5 per metre. How much does it cost to fence a plot 20 m long and 10 m wide?
quiz.mistake: Uses area (200 × 5 = ₹1000) or forgets to multiply by the rate (₹60)

teach.ask: Gappu wants to put twigs all around his nest: 'How do I find the perimeter?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Walk around the edge and add every side. Now I know how many twigs I need!
teach.nudge: What do I do with the lengths of the sides? And is it inside or around the shape?

learn.hook: How many tiles will cover your classroom floor? Area tells you how much surface a shape covers.
points: Area is the amount of surface a shape covers. We measure it in square units like cm² and m².
Count the unit squares inside, or use a rule: area of a rectangle = length × breadth.
Area of a square = side × side.
Use the same unit for both sides: don't multiply cm by m.
Area and perimeter are different: two shapes can have the same area but different perimeters.

example.q: A floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. How many 1 m × 1 m tiles cover it?

learn.reallife: Buying a carpet, painting a wall or planting grass on a lawn all depend on area.

games.title: Perimeter or area?
items: Lace around a tablecloth
Fence around a farm
Frame around a photo
Boundary rope of a cricket field
Carpet to cover a floor
Paint for a wall
Grass to cover a lawn
Tiles for a kitchen floor

quiz.q: Kabir's notebook cover is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area = length × breadth = 20 × 15 = 300 cm².
quiz.mistake: Works out perimeter (70) or adds the sides (35)

quiz.q: A square carrom board has side 70 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area of a square = side × side = 70 × 70 = 4900 cm².
quiz.mistake: Finds perimeter (280), doubles the side (140), or drops a zero (490)

quiz.q: A rectangle is made of 5 rows of unit squares with 7 squares in each row. What is its area?
quiz.explain: 5 rows of 7 squares = 5 × 7 = 35 unit squares.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 + 7 (12) or finds the perimeter (24)

quiz.q: A room floor is 6 m by 4 m. Tiles of 1 m × 1 m cost ₹50 each. How much does it cost to tile the floor?
quiz.explain: The floor needs 6 × 4 = 24 tiles. 24 × ₹50 = ₹1200.
quiz.mistake: Uses the perimeter, 20 m (₹1000), instead of the area

quiz.q: A rectangle has area 48 cm² and breadth 6 cm. What is its length?
quiz.explain: Length × 6 = 48, so length = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing (42)

quiz.q: Rectangle A is 6 cm × 4 cm. Rectangle B is 8 cm × 3 cm. Which is true?
quiz.explain: Both areas are 24 cm². The perimeters are 2 × 10 = 20 cm and 2 × 11 = 22 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal areas must mean equal perimeters

quiz.q: Aisha cuts a 10 cm × 10 cm square of paper into 1 cm × 1 cm squares. How many small squares does she get?
quiz.explain: 10 rows of 10 small squares make 10 × 10 = 100.
quiz.mistake: Counts only around the edge (40) or adds the sides (20)

quiz.q: A square has perimeter 20 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm, so area = 5 × 5 = 25 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the area equals the perimeter, or squares the perimeter (400)

teach.ask: Gappu wants to cover his nest floor with soft leaves: 'How do I work out the area?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Area is the space inside, length × breadth, in square units. My nest will be so cosy!
teach.nudge: Do I add or multiply the sides? And what units does area use?

topics.title: Area puzzles: triangles and odd shapes

learn.hook: Cut a sandwich corner to corner and each half has exactly half the area. That simple idea solves many puzzles!
points: A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two equal triangles, so each triangle has half the rectangle's area.
For shapes made of rectangles (like an L shape), split them into rectangles, find each area and add.
On a grid, count full squares as 1 and two half squares as 1 more.
Cutting a shape and rearranging the pieces without overlap keeps the same area. This is the idea behind the tangram.
To find an area with a hole, find the whole area and subtract the hole.

example.q: An L shape is made of a 6 cm × 2 cm rectangle and a 2 cm × 3 cm rectangle. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Working out paint for an L-shaped room or cloth for a triangular flag uses these tricks.

games.title: Match the shape to its area
pairs: Half of a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle
Half of a 10 cm × 3 cm rectangle
A 3 cm × 5 cm and a 2 cm × 2 cm rectangle joined
8 full grid squares and 4 half squares
One half of a 4 cm square cut along a diagonal

games.title: Area puzzle facts
items: A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two triangles of equal area.
The two triangles fit exactly on top of each other.
If you cut a shape and rearrange the pieces without overlapping, the area stays the same.
No paper is added or lost.
A shape with a bigger perimeter always has a bigger area.
A 1 cm × 9 cm rectangle has perimeter 20 cm but area 9 cm², less than a 4 cm × 4 cm square (perimeter 16 cm, area 16 cm²).
Two half squares on a grid together make 1 square unit.
Half + half = 1.
A triangle cut from a 4 cm × 6 cm rectangle along its diagonal has area 24 cm².
It has half the area: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².

quiz.q: A rectangular sheet 8 cm × 6 cm is cut along a diagonal. What is the area of each triangle?
quiz.explain: The rectangle's area is 8 × 6 = 48 cm². Each triangle is half: 24 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve (48) or halves twice (12)

quiz.q: An L-shaped room is made of a 5 m × 4 m part and a 3 m × 2 m part. What is its total area?
quiz.explain: 5 × 4 = 20 m² and 3 × 2 = 6 m². Together: 26 m².
quiz.mistake: Adds all the lengths (14) or counts only one part (20)

quiz.q: On a grid, a leaf covers 9 full squares and 6 half squares. What is its area?
quiz.explain: 6 half squares make 3 full squares. 9 + 3 = 12 square units.
quiz.mistake: Counts each half square as a whole square (15)

quiz.q: A square garden 10 m × 10 m has a square pond of side 2 m in it. What area is left for grass?
quiz.explain: Garden: 10 × 10 = 100 m². Pond: 2 × 2 = 4 m². Grass: 100 − 4 = 96 m².
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the pond's perimeter (8) instead of its area

quiz.q: A tangram square has area 16 cm². Riya uses all its pieces, without overlapping, to make a cat. What is the cat's area?
quiz.explain: Rearranging the same pieces does not change the area, so the cat is 16 cm².
quiz.mistake: Thinks a new shape must have a new area

quiz.q: A 2 cm × 2 cm square is cut out from the corner of a 12 cm × 5 cm rectangle. What is the area of what is left?
quiz.explain: 12 × 5 = 60 cm². The cut-out is 2 × 2 = 4 cm². 60 − 4 = 56 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the cut-out (60) or adds it (64)

quiz.q: Two triangles, each half of a 4 cm × 3 cm rectangle, are put together. What is their total area?
quiz.explain: Two halves make the whole rectangle: 4 × 3 = 12 cm².
quiz.mistake: Gives the area of only one triangle (6)

quiz.q: Joseph's T-shaped kite is made of a 6 cm × 2 cm top bar and a 2 cm × 5 cm stem. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Top bar: 6 × 2 = 12 cm². Stem: 2 × 5 = 10 cm². Total: 22 cm².
quiz.mistake: Adds all the lengths (15) or multiplies everything together (120)

teach.ask: Gappu has an L-shaped leaf: 'It's not a rectangle! How do I find its area?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Cut it into rectangles, find each area and add them up. Easy peasy!
teach.nudge: Can I break the shape into simpler pieces first? What do I do after that?

learn.hook: Fractions live between the whole numbers on the number line. Let's go and find their homes!
points: A fraction names equal parts of a whole: 3/4 means 3 of 4 equal parts.
To show 3/4 on a number line, split the gap from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts and take 3 jumps.
A fraction with a top bigger than the bottom, like 5/4, is more than 1. It lies between 1 and 2.
5/4 can be written as the mixed number 1 1/4 (one whole and one quarter).
Unit fractions get smaller as the bottom number grows: 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4, because the whole is cut into more pieces.

example.q: Where does 7/3 lie on the number line?
steps: 3 thirds make 1 whole, 6 thirds make 2 wholes.
So it lies between 2 and 3, one third of the way from 2.

learn.reallife: Recipes ask for 1 1/2 cups of rice, and running tracks are split into quarter laps.

quiz.q: The gap from 0 to 1 is split into 5 equal parts. Riya lands on the 3rd mark after 0. Which fraction is she on?
quiz.explain: Each part is 1/5, and 3 jumps of 1/5 make 3/5.
quiz.mistake: Flips the fraction (5/3) or uses the mark number as the bottom

quiz.q: Which is larger: 1/6 or 1/9?
quiz.explain: Cutting a whole into 6 parts gives bigger pieces than cutting it into 9 parts. So 1/6 > 1/9.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger bottom number means a bigger fraction

quiz.q: Write 13/4 as a mixed number.
quiz.explain: 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1, so 13/4 = 3 wholes and 1/4.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the numbers around (4 1/3) or writes the remainder wrongly

quiz.q: Arjun ran 2 3/5 km. Write this as an improper fraction.
quiz.explain: 2 wholes = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 13/5.
quiz.mistake: Writes the digits side by side (23/5) or forgets the 3 fifths (10/5)

quiz.q: Between which two whole numbers does 17/5 lie?
quiz.explain: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, so 17/5 = 3 2/5, which lies between 3 and 4.
quiz.mistake: Looks at only the top number (17)

quiz.q: On a number line, each whole is split into quarters. How many jumps of 1/4 does it take to reach 1 1/2 from 0?
quiz.explain: 1 whole is 4 quarters and 1/2 is 2 quarters, so 1 1/2 = 6 quarters: 6 jumps.
quiz.mistake: Counts the 1 as one jump, or counts halves instead of quarters (3)

quiz.q: Kabir shares 3 rotis equally among 4 friends. What fraction of a roti does each friend get?
quiz.explain: 3 rotis shared by 4 means 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 of a roti each.
steps: Cut each roti into 4 quarters: 12 quarters
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way round (4/3)

quiz.q: Which fraction is exactly equal to 1?
quiz.explain: 7/7 means all 7 of 7 equal parts, which is one whole. 7/1 is 7 wholes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 7/1 is one whole

teach.ask: Gappu hops on a number line: 'Where do I land for 3/4? It's not a whole number!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Split 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts and hop 3 times. I landed on 3/4!
teach.nudge: How should I cut up the gap from 0 to 1, and how many hops do I take?

learn.hook: Half a pizza or two quarters? Same amount of pizza, different names!
points: Equivalent fractions name the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8.
Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number to get an equivalent fraction: 2/3 = 8/12 (both × 4).
A fraction is in lowest terms when the top and bottom have no common factor except 1: 12/18 = 2/3 (both ÷ 6).
To compare fractions, change them to the same denominator: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so 3/4 is bigger.
Adding the same number to top and bottom does NOT give an equivalent fraction.

example.q: Write 18/24 in lowest terms.
steps: The greatest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6

learn.reallife: When you cut a cake into 8 slices and eat 4, you've eaten half, just as if it were cut into 2 and you ate 1.

items.text: 15/20 in lowest terms is ___
Multiply the top and bottom by the ___ number to get an equivalent fraction.
The bigger of 3/8 and 2/5 is ___

quiz.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 3/4?
quiz.explain: Multiply the top and bottom of 3/4 by 3: 9/12.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the bottom (3/8) or only the top

quiz.q: Write 24/36 in lowest terms.
quiz.explain: The greatest common factor of 24 and 36 is 12. 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Divides top and bottom by different numbers

quiz.q: Meena ate 2/8 of a pizza. Harpreet ate 1/4 of the same-sized pizza. Who ate more?
quiz.explain: 2/8 in lowest terms is 1/4, so they ate the same amount.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger numbers in the fraction mean more pizza

quiz.q: Which is bigger: 5/6 or 7/9?
quiz.explain: With denominator 18: 5/6 = 15/18 and 7/9 = 14/18. So 5/6 is bigger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the fraction with bigger numbers is bigger

quiz.q: Fill in the missing number: 4/7 = 20/?
quiz.explain: 4 × 5 = 20, so multiply the bottom by 5 too: 7 × 5 = 35.
quiz.mistake: Adds 20 to the bottom (27) or multiplies the bottom by 4 instead of 5 (28)

quiz.q: Aisha says 2/5 = 4/7 because she added 2 to the top and to the bottom. What is wrong?
options: She should add 2 only to the top
We must multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number, not add
quiz.explain: 2/5 = 4/10 (both × 2). Adding the same number changes the amount: 4/7 is bigger than 2/5.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding the same number to top and bottom keeps a fraction equal

quiz.q: Which is the smallest: 1/2, 2/3, 3/8 or 5/12?
quiz.mistake: Picks the fraction with the smallest top number without comparing properly

quiz.q: A chocolate bar has 12 equal pieces. Joseph eats 9 pieces. What fraction did he eat, in lowest terms?
quiz.explain: He ate 9/12. Divide top and bottom by 3: 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Gives the part left over (1/4) instead of the part eaten

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'How can 1/2 and 3/6 be equal? The numbers are different!'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! 1/2 × 3 on top and bottom gives 3/6. Same amount of mango, just cut smaller!
teach.nudge: What can I do to the top and bottom numbers without changing the amount?

learn.hook: Half a glass of lassi plus a quarter glass: how full is the glass? Let's add fractions!
points: Same denominator: add or subtract the tops and keep the bottom. 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.
Different denominators: first change to equivalent fractions with a common denominator. 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
Never add the bottoms! 1/2 + 1/2 is 1, not 2/4.
Mixed numbers: change to improper fractions first, or add the wholes and the parts separately.
Brahmagupta, an Indian mathematician who lived about 1400 years ago, wrote down rules for working with fractions like these.
learn.reallife: Cooking with 1/2 cup and 1/4 cup, or adding up pieces of a shared pizza, uses fraction addition.

games.title: Fraction sums: true or false?
items: Keep the denominator: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3.
Same denominator, so add the tops: 3 + 1 = 4.
To add 1/4 and 1/6 you can use 12 as a common denominator.
12 is a multiple of both 4 and 6.

quiz.q: Riya drinks 2/9 of a bottle of lassi in the morning and 4/9 in the evening. How much does she drink in all?
quiz.explain: 2/9 + 4/9 = 6/9, which is 2/3 in lowest terms.
quiz.mistake: Adds the bottoms too (6/18)
Adds tops and bottoms separately (2/7)

quiz.q: A ribbon is 7/8 m long. Kabir cuts off 3/8 m. How much ribbon is left?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting (10/8)

quiz.explain: 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12, so the difference is 1/12.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts tops and bottoms separately (1/1)

quiz.q: Arjun walks 1 1/2 km to school and then 2 1/4 km to the market. How far does he walk in total?
quiz.mistake: Adds the fraction parts by adding tops and bottoms (2/6)

quiz.q: Mother made 1 whole cake. 2/5 was eaten at lunch and 1/3 at tea time. What fraction is left?
quiz.mistake: Gives the part eaten (11/15) instead of the part left

quiz.q: What is the right first step for 2/3 + 1/4?
options: Add tops and bottoms to get 3/7
quiz.explain: 12 is a common multiple of 3 and 4. Then 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
quiz.mistake: Adds the denominators to make a 'common' denominator

quiz.q: Meena says 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8. What is the correct answer?
quiz.explain: Keep the denominator: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. (2/8 is only 1/4, which would mean the sum is no bigger than one part!)
quiz.mistake: Adds the denominators as well as the numerators

teach.ask: Gappu ate 1/2 a guava and then 1/3 of another one: 'How much guava did I eat altogether?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Change both to sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. I ate 5/6 of a guava. Yum!
teach.nudge: Can I add halves and thirds straight away, or do the pieces need to be the same size first?

learn.hook: With just a pencil, a ruler and a compass, you can draw perfect circles, arcs and amazing designs!
points: A ruler draws straight lines and measures lengths. A compass draws circles and arcs.
To use a compass: open it to the length you need, fix the sharp point at the centre, and turn the pencil all the way round.
Every point on a circle is the same distance from the centre. This distance is the radius, and the diameter is 2 × radius.
An arc is a part of a circle. With a compass you can copy a length: open it to the length, then mark the same length somewhere else.
Two arcs drawn from two different centres cross at a point that is at those exact distances from both centres.

example.q: AB is 6 cm. How do you find a point that is 4 cm from A and also 4 cm from B?
steps: Put the point on A and draw an arc above AB.
Without changing the opening, put the point on B and draw another arc.
Where the arcs cross, the point is 4 cm from both A and B.
example.answer: The crossing point of the two 4 cm arcs

learn.reallife: Kolam and rangoli artists use string or chalk like a compass, and engineers use compasses on maps to measure distances.

games.title: Draw a circle of radius 3 cm
items: Put the compass point at 0 on the ruler
Open the compass until the pencil tip is at 3 cm
Without changing the opening, press the compass point firmly on the paper where the centre should be
Turn the compass all the way round without changing the opening

games.title: Compass facts
items: A compass is used to draw circles and arcs.
That's its main job!
Every point on a circle is the same distance from the centre.
That distance is the radius.
If the compass opening slips while drawing, you still get a perfect circle.
The radius would change, so the curve would not be a circle.
The diameter is half the radius.
The diameter is twice the radius.
An arc is a part of a circle.
Like a slice of the circle's edge.
A ruler can measure the length of a line segment.
Line up 0 with one end and read the other.

quiz.q: Riya opens her compass to 5 cm and draws a circle. What is its diameter?
quiz.explain: The compass opening is the radius. Diameter = 2 × radius = 2 × 5 = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the opening is the diameter, or halves instead of doubling

quiz.q: A bangle has a diameter of 6 cm. What compass opening draws a circle the same size?
quiz.explain: The compass opening is the radius, which is half the diameter: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the diameter as the compass opening

quiz.q: Which tool is best for drawing a circle?
quiz.explain: A compass keeps the pencil the same distance from the centre as it turns.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the compass with the protractor, which measures angles

quiz.q: Arjun draws an arc of radius 4 cm with centre A, and another arc of radius 4 cm with centre B. They meet at P. How far is P from A?
quiz.explain: P lies on the arc with centre A and radius 4 cm, so P is exactly 4 cm from A.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two radii (8 cm)

quiz.q: Points X and Y are on a circle with centre O and radius 7 cm. What is OX + OY?
quiz.explain: OX and OY are both radii, so each is 7 cm. 7 + 7 = 14 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 7 × 7 (49) or counts only one radius

quiz.q: While drawing a circle with a compass, what must NOT change?
options: The opening between the point and the pencil
quiz.explain: If the opening changes, the radius changes and the curve is no longer a circle.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the compass opening to the radius

quiz.q: AB is 6 cm. Meena wants a point exactly 6 cm from both A and B. What compass opening should she use for both arcs?
quiz.explain: She wants the point 6 cm from A and 6 cm from B, so both arcs need a 6 cm opening. Joining the point to A and B makes a triangle with all sides 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves the length (3 cm), thinking of the middle of AB

quiz.q: Kabir opens his compass from P to Q, then puts the point on R and marks S with the same opening. What is true?
quiz.explain: The compass opening did not change, so RS is the same length as PQ.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise a compass can copy a length exactly

teach.ask: Gappu grips a compass with his claws: 'How do I draw a perfect round circle with this?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Fix the point at the centre, keep the opening the same, and turn all the way round. Perfect circle!
teach.nudge: Where do I put the sharp point, and what must stay the same while I turn?

learn.hook: Every rectangle has four perfect corners. Let's build one, step by step, and decorate with circles!
points: A rectangle has opposite sides equal and all four angles 90°. A square has all four sides equal and all angles 90°.
To draw a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle: draw AB = 6 cm, make 90° angles at A and B, mark 4 cm up from each end, then join the top points.
The diagonals of a rectangle join opposite corners. They are equal in length and cut each other into halves.
Circles with the same centre but different radii are called concentric circles, like ripples in a pond.
Always check: measure the sides and diagonals after drawing to see if your rectangle is accurate.

example.q: Draw a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm. What should its perimeter be?
steps: At P and Q, draw lines at 90°.
Mark S and R 3 cm up those lines.
Join SR; it should measure 5 cm.
example.answer: A rectangle with sides 5, 3, 5, 3 cm and perimeter 16 cm

learn.reallife: Cricket pitches, carrom boards and doors are rectangles; dartboards and archery targets are concentric circles.

games.title: Match the shape word to its meaning
pairs: All points the same distance from the centre

games.title: Always true for every rectangle?
items: All four angles are 90°
Opposite sides are equal
The two diagonals are equal
The diagonals cut each other into halves
All four sides are equal
The diagonals meet at right angles
Its length is double its breadth
It has only one right angle

quiz.q: Kabir draws a rectangle with one side 7 cm and the next side 4 cm. How long is the side opposite the 7 cm side?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so it is 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the opposite side equals the next side

quiz.q: How big is each corner angle of a rectangle?
quiz.explain: All four angles of a rectangle are right angles, 90° each.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a rectangle's corner with a straight angle

quiz.q: One diagonal of a rectangle is 10 cm long. How long is the other diagonal?
quiz.explain: The two diagonals of a rectangle are always equal, so it is 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the second diagonal is half or double the first

quiz.q: The diagonals of rectangle ABCD meet at O. If AC = 12 cm, how long is AO?
quiz.explain: The diagonals cut each other into halves, so AO = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that O is the middle of AC

quiz.q: Aisha draws circles with the same centre and radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. What are these circles called?
quiz.explain: Circles that share a centre are concentric circles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks circles with the same centre must be equal

quiz.q: Which steps draw a square of side 5 cm?
options: Draw two 5 cm lines anywhere and join them
Draw a circle of radius 5 cm
Draw a 5 cm line and a 10 cm line at 90°
Draw a 5 cm line, make 90° angles at both ends, mark 5 cm up each, then join
quiz.explain: A square needs four 5 cm sides and four right angles. The last set of steps gives exactly that.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the corners must be right angles

quiz.q: Harpreet draws a circle of radius 3 cm. She draws a second circle of radius 3 cm whose centre lies on the first circle. How far apart are the two centres?
quiz.explain: The second centre is on the first circle, so it is one radius, 3 cm, from the first centre.
quiz.mistake: Adds both radii (6 cm)

quiz.q: Joseph wants to draw a rectangle with perimeter 20 cm and one side 6 cm. Which pair of side lengths should he use?
quiz.explain: Length + breadth = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 cm, so the other side is 10 − 6 = 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 6 from 20 without halving (14 cm)

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a rectangle for his nest door: 'How do I make sure it's a real rectangle?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Measure with a ruler, make 90° corners, keep opposite sides equal. A perfect door!
teach.nudge: What must the corners be, and which sides have to be equal?

learn.hook: Fold a butterfly picture down the middle and both wings match perfectly. That's line symmetry!
points: A shape has line symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that the two halves match exactly.
The fold line is called the line of symmetry (or axis of symmetry). Each half is a mirror image of the other.
Some shapes have many lines of symmetry: a rectangle has 2, an equilateral triangle 3, a square 4 and a circle has unlimited lines.
A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry. A regular hexagon has 6.
Capital letters: A and M have a vertical line, B and E a horizontal line, H and X have both, and F, G, J and R have none.

example.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
steps: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides.
Each line of symmetry goes through one corner and the middle of the opposite side.

learn.reallife: The Taj Mahal, rangoli designs, leaves and many temple doors are symmetrical.
